subject: paediatrics
title: Upper Airway Emergencies: Croup, Epiglottitis and Empyema

steps.tx: Subglottic tracheal mucosal inflammation produces acute pediatric stridor and characteristic coughing. The most frequent cause of infectious upper airway obstruction in children aged six months to three years is **acute viral croup**, or laryngotracheobronchitis, caused predominantly by parainfluenza virus type 1. Viral replication provokes inflammatory mucosal oedema of the cricoid cartilage ring, narrowing the narrowest anatomical region of the pediatric airway.
steps.say: Viral croup caused by parainfluenza virus type one narrows the subglottic airway in toddlers. It features a barking seal-like cough, hoarseness, and inspiratory stridor worsening at night.

vis.alt: Frontal neck radiograph showing the classic steeple sign of subglottic tracheal narrowing.
vis.caption: Subglottic tracheal stenosis producing the pathognomonic pencil-point steeple sign on frontal neck radiography. [Credit: StewardMD]

steps.tx: Frontal soft tissue radiography of the neck confirms subglottic tracheal narrowing. Radiography demonstrates symmetrical tapering of the subglottic airway column, designated as the **steeple sign radiograph**, or pencil-point sign, caused by circumferential mucosal oedema within the rigid cricoid ring. In contrast, the supraglottic structures, including the epiglottis and aryepiglottic folds, remain entirely normal and non-oedematous.
steps.say: Frontal neck X-rays reveal symmetrical subglottic narrowing called the steeple sign. Circumferential cricoid oedema tapers the tracheal air column like a church spire.

rows: Steeple sign on AP neck film
Thumbprint sign on lateral neck film

steps.tx: Systemic corticosteroids represent the cornerstone of pharmaceutical management for all croup severities. A single dose of oral or intramuscular **dexamethasone therapy** (0.15 to 0.6 mg/kg) reduces subglottic capillary permeability, shortens illness duration, and prevents endotracheal intubation. In moderate to severe croup with resting stridor, nebulized L-adrenaline (racemic epinephrine) provides rapid mucosal vasoconstriction, though patients require four hours of observation to monitor for rebound stridor.
steps.say: Dexamethasone is the cornerstone therapy for croup, reducing subglottic swelling. Nebulized adrenaline provides rapid temporary relief for resting stridor, requiring four hours of observation.

left.title: Systemic Dexamethasone
points: Single oral/IM dose (0.15 to 0.6 mg/kg)
Onset within 1 to 2 hours; lasts 48 to 72 hours
Effective in mild, moderate, and severe croup
Dramatically reduces hospital admission rates

right.title: Nebulized L-Adrenaline (Epinephrine)
points: Dose: 0.5 mL/kg of 1:1000 solution (max 5 mL)
Alpha-1 vasoconstriction shrinks oedema in 10 min
Effect wanes after 2 hours; potential rebound
Observe for 4 hours minimum before discharge

steps.tx: Fulminant supraglottic bacterial cellulitis creates a catastrophic risk of fatal airway obstruction. The life-threatening emergency **acute bacterial epiglottitis** involves severe inflammation of the epiglottis and arytenoid folds, historically caused by Haemophilus influenzae type b. Children aged two to seven years present acutely with high fever, toxic appearance, severe sore throat, pooling of saliva, and a muffled hot potato voice, sitting upright and tripoding.
steps.say: Acute epiglottitis is a medical emergency causing toxic fever, severe dysphagia, drooling, and a hot potato voice. Children sit tripoding forward with the neck extended.

vis.alt: Lateral soft tissue neck radiograph demonstrating the thumbprint sign of an enlarged swollen epiglottis.
vis.caption: Lateral neck radiograph showing severe swelling of the epiglottis producing the classic thumbprint sign. [Credit: StewardMD]

steps.tx: Lateral soft tissue radiography reveals massive enlargement of the supraglottic cartilage. Radiographs demonstrate the classic **thumb sign epiglottitis**, where the swollen, rounded, cherry-red epiglottis projects into the hypopharyngeal air shadow resembling an adult thumb. The cardinal clinical rule states that no attempt should be made to examine the pharynx with a tongue depressor outside the operating room, as this can trigger immediate fatal reflex laryngospasm.
steps.say: Lateral neck films reveal a swollen epiglottis resembling a thumbprint. Never inspect the pharynx with a tongue depressor outside an operating theatre, as it can trigger fatal laryngospasm.

rows: Absent cough, muffled hot potato voice
Immediate intubation in OR, IV ceftriaxone

steps.tx: Purulent bacterial collection in the pleural space complicates necrotizing bacterial pneumonias. Infection with Streptococcus pneumoniae or Staphylococcus aureus frequently progresses to **parapneumonic empyema**, characterized by persistent high fever, pleuritic chest pain, dullness to percussion, and decreased breath sounds over the affected hemithorax. Ultrasound confirms fibrinous septations, and management requires prompt chest tube drainage with intrapleural fibrinolytics or video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery alongside intravenous antibiotics.
steps.say: Empyema features purulent fluid in the pleural space, causing persistent fever, stony dullness, and reduced breath sounds. Management requires chest tube drainage and intravenous antibiotics.

left.title: Pleural Fluid Analysis in Empyema
points: Macroscopic appearance: frank cloudy pus
Pleural fluid pH <7.20 and glucose <40 mg/dL
Markedly elevated LDH (>1000 IU/L)
Positive Gram stain and bacterial culture

right.title: Thoracic Interventions
points: Intercostal pigtail or wide-bore chest tube
Intrapleural fibrinolytics (urokinase/tPA)
Video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery (VATS)
Intravenous co-amoxiclav or ceftriaxone

steps.tx: Staphylococcal pneumonia in young infants characteristically forms thin-walled intrapulmonary air cysts. Necrotizing bronchiolar ulceration by Staphylococcus aureus creates check-valve airway obstruction, producing **staphylococcal pneumatocele cysts**. These thin-walled, air-filled parenchymal cavities expand progressively under positive alveolar pressure and may rupture into the pleural cavity, triggering sudden tension pyopneumothorax. Most uncomplicated pneumatoceles resolve spontaneously over several months without requiring surgical resection.
steps.say: Staphylococcal pneumonia produces thin-walled pneumatoceles through check-valve bronchiolar damage. While they risk tension pyopneumothorax, uncomplicated cysts resolve spontaneously over months.

vis.alt: Radiographic view of pediatric neck and thoracic cavities.
vis.caption: Radiological comparison of pediatric upper airway narrowing and thoracic parenchymal lesions. [Credit: StewardMD]

steps.tx: Suppurative infection of the potential space between pharynx and prevertebral fascia presents with torticollis. A **retropharyngeal abscess** typically affects toddlers following an upper respiratory infection with extension into retropharyngeal lymph nodes. Children present with high fever, painful limitation of neck extension (torticollis), drooling, muffled phonation, and posterior pharyngeal bulging. Lateral neck radiographs show prevertebral soft tissue widening exceeding the width of adjacent cervical vertebrae.
steps.say: Retropharyngeal abscess causes high fever, painful neck stiffness, drooling, and prevertebral soft tissue widening on lateral X-rays. Intravenous antibiotics and surgical drainage are definitive.

left.title: Prevertebral Space Criteria
points: C2-C4 level: prevertebral width >7 mm
C6 level: width >14 mm in children (<22 mm adult)
Exceeds width of adjacent vertebral body
Obtain true lateral neck film in extension

right.title: Definitive Management
points: Intravenous ampicillin-sulbactam or ceftriaxone
Transoral incision and drainage in operating room
Secure endotracheal intubation with cuff protection
Airway monitoring until oedema resolves
